summary: Doug Ford sets conditions for any US trade deal, the Pentagon publicly criticizes Canada's military, Taiwan presses Ottawa to sign a trade pact, and the Bank of Canada governor speaks in Toronto today.
body: Ontario Premier Doug Ford said on Monday he will not support a Canada-US trade deal unless the auto, steel and manufacturing industries first approve it.[^1] Ottawa is seeking an interim deal that would cut US tariffs before the larger review of CUSMA, the North American trade agreement. Global News reports that in August the US offered to lower the tariff on Canadian cars from 25% to 15%, which carmakers and unions said would still hurt. The US trade chief calls a deal "fairly close", while Canada's negotiator says several issues are unresolved.[^1]

The Pentagon released a "fact sheet" on Monday saying Canada's military is not ready enough and has not made the hard choices to meet its NATO spending pledge. It came a week after a memo from US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth limiting some contact between the two militaries.[^2] Defence Minister David McGuinty says it is "business as usual". Canada reached NATO's 2% of GDP target for the first time in 2025 and plans to spend much more by 2030.[^2]

Taiwan's deputy foreign minister, visiting Ottawa, urged Canada to sign a trade deal whose talks ended in March 2025, saying it could help protect Canada from pressure by Beijing. Prime Minister Mark Carney says he hopes it will be signed soon.[^3] In Question Period, Conservatives called a $2.2-million federal grant to a biomass company run by AI Minister Evan Solomon's brother "self-dealing"; the government says the minister recused himself and no minister made the decision.[^4]
Today Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem speaks at the Economic Club of Canada in Toronto at about 12:40 p.m. on the economy and interest rates. The next rate decision is Dec 9.[^5][^6]
differences: On trade, Washington sounds upbeat while Canada stresses open issues.[^1] On defence, the Pentagon says Canada lags; McGuinty calls it "business as usual", and former Conservative leader Erin O'Toole says the fact sheet ignores the past year.[^2] On the grant, Conservatives allege a conflict of interest; the government and the company say the process was independent.[^4]
